title: The summer solstice
hookLine: the longest day, and Marcus would note it passes too

lines: IT SEEMS TO GO ON FOREVER.
cards: Nine-thirty at night, and it's still light enough to read on the back step. Kids are still out on bikes. Somebody's grill is still going.
In the far north, in places like northern Norway, the sun doesn't set at all this time of year. The summer solstice: the longest day in the northern half of the world.

People have lit bonfires for it, danced around poles for it, stayed up all night for it. The light seems like it could go on forever. Marcus Aurelius would enjoy it, and then gently remind himself of one thing.

teach.b: First, the word. Solstice comes from Latin, solstitium: the sun standing still.
For days around it, the sun seems to rise and set at almost the same points on the horizon, as if pausing at the top of its climb before turning back.

teach.h: THE PEAK IS ALSO THE TURN.
teach.b: Second, the pause is the turn. From tomorrow, in the north, the days begin to shorten, a little at a time. The peak of the light and the start of its going are the same moment.

teach.h: A RIVER OF THINGS, SWEPT PAST.
teach.b: He writes that time is like a river made of things that happen, a strong current: as soon as something is seen, it's swept away, something else takes its place, and that too will be carried off.
He tells himself to think often about how fast everything that exists is carried past and out of sight. To some readers that sounds bleak.

But read beside his other notes, it isn't a reason to hold back from enjoying things. It's a reason to enjoy them now, while they're here, without trying to clamp them in place. Fourth, the solstice as practice.
A long day can seem so roomy that it slips by unnoticed.

teach.h: PASSING, SO WORTH BEING OUT IN.
teach.b: Marcus's reminder turns that around: because it's passing, it's worth being out in.
Both halves are true, and the second makes the first worth more.

how: Many cultures mark midsummer with bonfires, outdoor gatherings or staying up through the short night; some readers of Marcus use the longest day as a reminder to enjoy what is passing.

games.q: it's the longest evening of the year and you're about to spend it indoors on your phone. what would Marcus's river remind you?
o: there's plenty more light, no hurry

games.why: everything is swept past like a river; that's a reason to be present for it now.

practice: Go outside if you can, or sit by the window with the most sky, and look at the light as it is right now: its color, where the shadows fall, how warm or cool the air is. Enjoy it fully, without planning anything.
Then notice, quietly, that this exact light is already moving across the wall, the ground, your hand, and enjoy it anyway, partly because it's passing.

wordCard.voice: Solstitium, Latin for the sun standing still, the root of solstice, the longest day when the light pauses before it turns. Today's word.
